composition: A binary Fe-Al low-density steel with a nominal aluminium content of 5 wt% (designated Fe-5Al), the balance being Fe. The alloy was prepared from charges of interstitial free (IF) steel and pure aluminium. Adding Al to Fe up to ~10 wt% stabilizes the body-centred cubic (BCC) ferrite phase and lowers density; at 5 wt% Al (which gives ~8% density reduction at higher Al levels) a single ferrite phase is retained. Al is non-magnetic and resides either in solid solution in the ferrite lattice or in the ordered phase, altering the local Fe atomic environment. No other alloying elements are reported for this sample. For the binary Fe-Al system, solid-solution strengthening was estimated to rise from 67.8 MPa at 5 wt% Al to 127.2 MPa at 9 wt% Al.
conclusions: Within the paper's study of strengthening in Fe-Al ferritic low-density steels, the Fe-5Al powder sample shows that a binary Fe-Al alloy with only 5 wt% Al already contains a nano-sized Fe3Al (DO3) ordered phase dispersed in single-phase BCC ferrite, although both its size (~2.5 ± 0.15 nm) and its volume fraction (just below 0.5%) are the smallest of the Fe-Al series investigated (5–9 wt% Al), where the ordered-phase size increases from 2.5 ± 0.15 to 3.75 ± 0.2 nm with Al content. The Mössbauer data show that Al is present both in solid solution and as an ordered phase and that the local Fe environment is progressively modified by Al. Overall, the paper concludes that nano-sized Fe3Al order (characterized by TEM, SAXS and Mössbauer spectroscopy) together with dislocation and grain-size strengthening accounts for the enhanced yield strength of Fe-Al based low-density steels; the ordered phase was achieved without major alloying additions.
mechanisms: Addition of non-magnetic Al to the BCC Fe lattice changes the local Fe atomic configuration, so the ⁵⁷Fe hyperfine magnetic field decreases as the number of Al nearest neighbours increases, following B = B0 − n1·ΔB1 − n2·ΔB2 (B0 = 33 T, ΔB1 = 2.4 T, ΔB2 = 0.5 T); this produces the broadened, multi-component Mössbauer sextet of Fe-5Al relative to the α-Fe foil.

In Fe-5Al the dominant 30.6 T Mössbauer component can arise either from the local configuration (7Fe+1Al)nn + (6Fe)nnn or from the Fe3Al (DO3) configuration (8Fe)nn + (6Al)nnn; the closeness of the two peaks prevents them from being separated.

Fe3Al has an additional hyperfine-field component ((4Fe+4Al)nn + (6Fe)nnn) near ~21 T, so the ~23 T peak seen in Fe-6Al, Fe-6.8Al and Fe-9Al is a possible indicator of a low-volume-fraction Fe3Al phase; its absence in Fe-5Al is attributed to the low volume fraction of Fe3Al in this composition.

SAXS scattering from the nano-sized ordered phase appears as a weak peak between q = 0.3–3 nm⁻¹; with increasing Al content the scattering intensity rises (more ordered phase) and the Guinier region shifts to lower q (larger ordered-phase size), reflecting the increasing driving force for ordering with Al addition.
The q⁻⁴ (Porod) decay of the SAXS intensity below q = 0.3 nm⁻¹ originates from larger heterogeneities such as grains and/or grain boundaries, not from the ordered phase itself.

SAXS volume fractions of the ordered phase are lower than the DO3 volume fractions traced by Mössbauer spectroscopy, because SAXS senses collectively the ordered phase having a sharper boundary, whereas Mössbauer spectroscopy traces all local environments including those with diffused boundaries.
microstructure: Polycrystalline, single-phase ferrite (BCC, disordered Fe-Al matrix) containing a nano-sized Fe3Al ordered phase with the DO3 structure — i.e. a two-phase structure, with stabilization of the single ferrite phase upon 5 wt% Al addition. The Fe3Al ordered phase is nano-sized and spherical (a spherical form factor was assumed in the SAXS model); at the 5 wt% Al composition SAXS gives an ordered-phase diameter of ~2.5 ± 0.15 nm and a volume fraction just below 0.5%, the smallest size and fraction of the Fe-Al series investigated. The SAXS profile shows a weak nano-sized ordered-phase scattering peak between q = 0.3–3 nm⁻¹; at low q (below 0.3 nm⁻¹) the intensity decays as q⁻⁴ (Porod scattering), assigned to larger heterogeneities such as grains/grain boundaries, while at high q (> 3 nm⁻¹) an incoherent flat background appears. No grain-size, texture or defect data are reported specifically for this powder sample.
processing: Step 1 – Vacuum arc melting (alloy preparation): charges of IF steel and pure aluminium were melted in a vacuum arc furnace; the resulting circular buttons (diameter 10 cm, height 5 cm) were re-melted 7–8 times to remove segregation, producing the Fe-5Al (5 wt% Al) low-density steel. Step 2 – Filing (mechanical processing): the alloy was filed to obtain powder for the Mössbauer and SAXS measurements; filing generates internal stress in the powder particles. Step 3 – Annealing (heat treatment): the powder was wrapped in copper foil, sealed in a glass tube under high vacuum (10⁻⁵ mBar) and annealed at 600 °C for 60 min; this anneal was performed specifically to remove the internal stress generated during creation of the powder particles by filing.
properties: No mechanical-test properties are reported for the Fe-5Al powder sample; its characterization was spectroscopic/scattering. Mössbauer spectroscopy (room temperature, transmission geometry, conventional constant-acceleration Doppler drive with a ⁵⁷Co (Rh-matrix) source, velocity calibrated with a pure α-Fe foil, spectra fitted with the NORMOS program using a hyperfine-field (B_hf) distribution of up to 40 sextets) resolved the Fe-5Al spectrum into two components: B_hf = 32.67 T (area 24%, V_f 23.55%, assigned (8Fe)nn + (5Fe+1Al)nnn) and B_hf = 30.65 T (area 51.6%, V_f 50.7%, assigned (7Fe+1Al)nn + (6Fe)nnn or (8Fe)nn + (6Al)nnn). Its P(B_hf) hump is broad and deconvoluted into multiple peaks spanning roughly 26–34 T, with envelope maxima near 30.5 and 33 T. SAXS (laboratory-based dual-energy Mo-Cr-SAXS system, Xeuss/Xenocs, France; camera lengths 550 and 2400 mm; q-range 0.0254–10 nm⁻¹; powder sandwiched between Scotch Magic tape; 2D profiles azimuthally integrated to 1D with FIT2D; absolute-scale conversion against glassy-carbon secondary standard; scattering angle calibrated with Silver-Behenate; measurement time 4–6 h) confirmed the nano-sized ordered phase and gave the diameter and volume fraction listed above.
summary: The Fe-5Al powder sample is a binary Fe-Al low-density steel containing 5 wt% Al, prepared from interstitial-free (IF) steel and pure aluminium by vacuum arc melting, then filed into powder and annealed at 600 °C for 60 min in high vacuum to relieve the internal stress introduced by filing. It was characterized by Mössbauer spectroscopy and small-angle X-ray scattering (SAXS) to resolve the local Fe atomic configuration and to quantify the nano-sized Fe3Al (DO3) ordered phase in the single-phase ferrite matrix, as part of a wider study of the strengthening mechanisms operating in Fe-Al based ferritic low-density steels.
unmapped: The Fe-5Al Mössbauer spectrum is a broadened six-line sextet relative to the α-Fe foil, evidencing that Al addition alters the local Fe atomic configurations and creates new, lower hyperfine-field components (figure_001).

The ~23 T Mössbauer hyperfine-field peak observed for Fe-6Al, Fe-6.8Al and Fe-9Al (a possible indicator of Fe3Al with a low volume fraction) is absent for Fe-5Al, which the authors attribute to the low volume fraction of the Fe3Al phase in Fe-5Al (b0047).

SAXS scattering intensity of the Fe-Al low-density steels increases with Al content (5→9 wt%), and the Guinier regions shift to low q, indicating increasing size of the nano-sized ordered phase; the q⁻⁴ decay below 0.3 nm⁻¹ indicates larger heterogeneities such as grains/grain boundaries (b0050).

The composition of the material after heat treatment was examined by wavelength dispersive spectroscopy (WDS) in a JEOL JXA-8530F electron probe micro-analyzer at 15 kV, and density was measured by Archimedes' principle (reported in Ref. [15]); the values are not reproduced for this sample in the paper text.
